analysis.one_liner: Rescinds remaining Inflation Reduction Act funding for IRS tax enforcement and operations.
analysis.headline: With zero cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in September 2022 and never received a vote, leaving the IRS enforcement funding intact.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would cancel the unspent portions of the money Congress gave the IRS in the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 for two things: enforcement (audits and collection against taxpayers who underpay) and operations support (staff, technology, and service infrastructure). The money was appropriated for a ten-year window, so most of it was still unspent when the bill was introduced. Canceling it would shrink the IRS's ability to audit complex, high-dollar returns and collect taxes that are owed but not paid.
analysis.who_benefits: Wealthy households and businesses with complex returns and large partnerships would face less audit and collection risk if the enforcement funding were canceled. The money for operations support also pays for answering taxpayer calls and processing returns, so cutting it would degrade service for everyone.

how_it_helps.text: The bill rescinds the unobligated balances of the IRS enforcement appropriation in section 10301 of the Inflation Reduction Act, removing funds designated for audits and collection work.
It also rescinds the unobligated operations support appropriation, which covers the IRS's staff, technology, and administrative capacity.
Fewer enforcement dollars mean fewer audits of complex, high-dollar returns, where underpayment is concentrated, reducing the risk of additional tax owed for those filers.

analysis.who_pays: Honest taxpayers would pay in two ways: less revenue collected from those who underpay means either more borrowing or higher taxes on everyone else, and cuts to operations support mean slower service, unanswered calls, and delayed refunds for ordinary filers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Honest filers and the public treasury

drawbacks.text: The bill's savings would come entirely from enforcement and administration, not tax rates, so the cost shows up as uncollected revenue that honest filers and federal borrowers effectively cover.
Cutting operations support would reduce the IRS's ability to serve taxpayers at all, including the phone and processing functions ordinary filers rely on, not just audit capacity.

The underlying appropriations run across a ten-year window, so a one-time rescission of 'unobligated' balances is largely a statement about future years' staffing and audit plans rather than a cut to current-year spending.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the wealthy taxpayers facing complex audits, the bill removes a real risk. For everyone else, the trade is one-sided: no tax cut, weaker taxpayer service, and uncollected revenue that shifts to honest filers or the deficit. It was not paired with any offsetting measure to protect taxpayer services, which even supporters of tighter IRS oversight generally acknowledge is a real cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Finance Committee in September 2022 and died there when the Congress ended in January 2023, without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.

narrative.text: Sen. Rick Scott introduced the bill on September 7, 2022, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee.
No cosponsors ever joined the bill.
No further action was recorded in the Senate before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the rescission never took effect and the enforcement and operations funding stayed in place.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary taxpayers and the public treasury came out ahead: the ten-year enforcement and operations funding that would have been canceled remains available, keeping audit capacity aimed at high-dollar underpayment and service levels intact. Wealthy and complex filers gained nothing because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Honest taxpayers and the public treasury

for.name: Sen. Rick Scott
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 7, 2022, to rescind the IRS enforcement and operations support funding.

against.name: Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill up in committee; it sat without a markup or hearing from September 2022 until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: One Republican introduced the bill with zero cosponsors, and the Democratic-run Finance Committee never acted on it; no roll-call vote ever occurred.

industries.industry: High-income households and large partnerships with complex returns
industries.note: Had it passed, the bill would have shrunk the audit and collection dollars aimed at complex, high-dollar filings, where underpayment is concentrated, lowering these filers' risk of paying taxes they owed. Honest filers would absorb the difference through higher deficits or taxes.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and advisory firms serving wealthy clients
industries.note: Less IRS enforcement capacity means fewer examinations and disputes, reducing one driver of demand for these firms' audit-defense work, while clients' ongoing planning needs remain.
